When I presented this report to the Chancellor, he responded with unexpected anger. This reaction revealed a critical vulnerability in the leadership of great statesmen. Reflecting on historical decisions, such as the Congress of Berlin and the Kulturkampf, I believe they were flawed from the start. The structure of the Empire’s constitution was tailored to fit the Chancellor’s dominance, but such grand ambitions do not suit everyone.
I emphasized the urgent need to develop a naval fleet promptly to safeguard our overseas interests. Since the Chancellor had already raised our flag abroad and gained public support, it was imperative that our navy stood firmly behind it. Unfortunately, the Chancellor dismissed these warnings, relying on his motto that any foreign incursion on our soil would be met with immediate force. He believed our colonies could be defended from the homeland alone.
Upon my return, both my grandfather and the Chancellor commended me for my straightforward report, which was a relief given my concerns about disappointing these influential figures. From Russia’s perspective, Disraeli’s diplomacy had transformed the Chancellor’s impartial role into an alliance favoring Anglo-Austrian interests over Russian ones.
The Foreign Office functioned merely as an extension of the Chancellor’s will, executing his directives without deviation. I assured my grandmother, from whom I’ve learned much through her lengthy reign, that I remained her devoted grandson and valued her counsel deeply. Yet, when it came to matters affecting our nation, I insisted on maintaining my independence of judgment.
Following the protocol of mourning, I planned my first visit to her and to England, honoring her as my grandmother and England as my mother’s homeland, before considering other destinations. The Chancellor, however, abruptly left the room during this discussion and attempted to draft a response to the Queen himself.
This approach is particularly relevant when examining industrial systems like Belgium’s, which mercilessly exploit their workforce without regard for the declining morale of their people. I frequently visited the residences of the Chancellor and Count Herbert, gaining deeper insight into the inner circle.
As I grew closer to the Bismarck faction, candid conversations about Herr von Holstein became common. He was connected to many individuals across social classes, all of whom respected him—and whom I treated with equal friendship and appreciation.
Despite my intentions, some members of this circle remained suspicious and distant toward me. They failed to transfer their loyalty from father to son, which hindered efforts to advance the welfare of our homeland.
